_readme: The signal sources shipped with the product. This is data: rewrite it,
extend it and switch entries off without recompiling anything.
To add one: put a `.json` file in `~/.config/sailor/triggers.d/` (or wherever
SAILOR_TRIGGER_DESCRIPTORS points) holding an array of descriptors, or an
object with a `triggers` field. An `id` already present here is replaced by
yours; to remove one, rewrite its `id` with `"disabled": true`.
`kind` is `manual` (somebody presses and it starts, carrying a text),
`terminal` (the signal would appear in a terminal session) or `periodic`
(the clock is the source). A terminal must
say in `listen` where it would be seen appearing: `appended_lines` for a file
that grows and is never rewritten, one JSON line per message;
`cursor_command` for a command that, given a cursor, prints what appeared
after it.
A periodic one must declare `periodic`, and there is no default for any of
its three fields: `every` ({"kind": "every_seconds", "seconds": 1800} or
{"kind": "daily_at", "hour": 3, "minute": 0}), `missed_run`
(`catch_up_each_one` or `once_for_all_of_them` — twelve hours asleep on a
half-hour source is twenty-four missed runs, and which answer is right
depends on the job), and `at_most_at_once` (at least 1). A descriptor that
leaves one out does not load, and the message names the field.
CAREFUL, AND IT HOLDS FOR EVERY `terminal` ENTRY: Sailor listens to no
terminal today. These entries declare the shape, and a step using one stops
and says what is missing. The same holds for `periodic`: the clock is kept —
the window beats every minute and `sailor flow tick` judges the same way —
but both read the flow's `schedule`, not this declaration, so such a step
stops too. Only `manual` really works, and none is shipped periodic.

triggers.label: By hand
triggers.note: Somebody presses and it starts, carrying a text. This is the launch button's source: the signal arrives together with the run, so there is nothing to wait for.

triggers.label: A session says something happened
triggers.note: Every command line Sailor grafts already calls `sailor session event` when a person submits a prompt, when a turn ends, and when a context is about to be compacted. That call is the source: after it has written its row it looks for the flows declaring this trigger, and starts them detached. What a flow asks of the event — its name, a phrase in the person's own prompt, the tree — is written in the trigger step's `on`, not here, because two flows watch the same call for different reasons.

triggers.label: Sailor's own terminal
triggers.note: The terminal engine exists now — `crates/terminal` — but NOBODY WRITES THIS FILE, and the path above is still the shape it will have rather than a measurement. That is a choice, not an oversight: a terminal running in the same process hands its routed request straight to the `manual` trigger, which carries the signal with it, and going through a file would be writing in order to read yourself back. This entry serves the case that does not exist yet: a terminal in ANOTHER process, which has to get its request to a Sailor living elsewhere. For that, the two things written in `trigger::action` are still missing — a process that stays up waiting, and a reader that keeps the point it reached.

triggers.label: Orca's panes
triggers.note: Sailor reads a host terminal only by the road that host publishes. For this one that is its documented read command, which returns text and takes a cursor; a terminal's own log file is written for its own redraw, may change without notice, and reading it is how an integration breaks on somebody else's release. It needs a tool descriptor with id `orca`, which is not shipped: add it in ~/.config/sailor/tools.d/.
